# Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being {.unnumbered}

Imagine choosing between a secure job and a new venture. The job protects a dependable income; the venture offers independence while putting that income at risk. Even with a clear forecast of success, you must give up something you value. And the option that feels exciting today must eventually fit an ordinary working week. How should a choice account for both the future we imagine and the life we will actually live?

This part connects uncertain outcomes to the lives in which they occur. It starts with the comparison of risky options and shows why a gain or loss depends partly on the point from which it is judged. It then asks how learning from experience differs from reading probabilities, why future plans can lose their appeal when action is due, and how mental accounts shape the use of money.

The habit chapter brings these questions into an ordinary afternoon, when a student keeps checking his phone while trying to write. The final chapter widens the lens: a decision that looks attractive in advance may contribute differently to daily experience, satisfaction, relationships, and meaning.

## Questions to carry forward

- What consequences am I comparing, and from which reference point?
- What changes between making a plan and carrying it out?
- What aspect of life is this decision meant to improve?

Many of those consequences depend on other people. Part IV examines choices whose outcomes are shaped by what others believe, value, and do.
